v.rationale:
Both suites pass: impl-1 has 52 tests, impl-2 has 31. Both builds use the same overall design: FormRequests for listing and admin, #[Scope] query scopes, a ProductSort enum, withQueryString pagination, a layout component with inline CSS, and to_route with flash. They also share one real bug. Because the listing request validates its filters, a bad query string on the public GET page redirects, and two different invalid URLs in a row loop forever. Both probes reproduced this and ran out of memory.

impl-1 ranks first because its Blade work is more complete and consistent. It has a full set of reusable form components (including checkbox and error), and the shared form is a real component. It uses @session flash, translatable strings, and field-level errors on the filter form too. Admins can edit the slug, with unique-ignore validation, and blank slugs are generated from the name. Its tests are much richer: describe blocks, datasets with exact validation messages, a selected category kept after a failed submit, and an access matrix. Its weak points are a MySQL-unsafe escape '\\' in raw SQL, building enum options in the view, and a fragile <ul> opened through $loop.

impl-2 has good global hygiene (shouldBeStrict, Paginator::defaultView, Gate) and a nice field wrapper built on slots. Against that, its shared form is an @include partial that declares @props. The filter form and the is_active checkbox are hand-written instead of reusing its own components. The slug is hidden from admins and handled through model hooks with a query loop. An unused Category slug hook adds clutter. Strings are hardcoded, filter errors appear only at the top of the page, and validating ?page adds another way to trigger the redirect bug.

A clean 31-test Pest suite covering authorisation for guests and non-admins, LIKE-wildcard escaping, sorting, pagination with filters preserved, 404 for inactive products, related products, and slug mass-assignment protection

v.rationale: Both suites pass (impl-2 31 tests, impl-1 52 tests), and the two are architecturally very similar: an enum for sort, an index FormRequest, #[Scope] scopes, a paginator with withQueryString, inline CSS, and a gate on the admin routes. The ranking turns on correctness in the form handling. impl-1's checkbox has no hidden fallback input. A probe showed that unticking 'Active' and then failing validation brings the box back ticked, because old() falls back to the model's value; impl-1's own test hides this by posting is_active => null. impl-1 also makes admins pick a unique slug by hand when names collide. impl-2 handles both cases correctly (a hidden 0 input, and automatic unique slugs). impl-2's flaws are smaller: it over-validates ?page (page=abc redirects), its shared form is an @include partial that declares @props rather than a true component, and it shows filter errors only at the top. impl-1 does have the nicer Blade component design (a real <x-product-form>, an <x-form.error> component, @session, policy-based can:) and the richer tests. Still, a real UX bug in the core form requirement ('keep previously entered input') weighs more heavily, so impl-2 ranks first.

v.rationale:
The two implementations are nearly identical in structure: an enum-cast status, an observer for the slug and published_at, scopes using the #[Scope] attribute, route-level ->can() authorization, a JsonResource that returns tag names, and paginated, newest-first index queries. Both pass their own suites (impl-1: 30 tests, impl-2: 31 tests).

My probes found:
- Both return 401 to guests, with or without a JSON Accept header.
- Both keep the existing published_at when a post is unpublished and then republished.
- impl-1 returns 422 for blank filters such as ?status=&tag=. impl-2 marks the filters nullable, returns 200, and tests this.
- impl-2 binds posts by slug and uses createOrFirst, which is safe when two requests create the same tag at once.
- impl-2's 'distinct' rule rejects duplicate tags with a 422, while impl-1 silently de-duplicates them. Either is defensible, but impl-2's rule clashes with its own de-duplication in syncTagNames.

impl-1 has the more elegant scopes (nullable parameters handled inside the scope) and slightly simpler routes. impl-2 avoids the blank-filter 422 and the tag-creation race, and reuses its validation rules by extending StorePostRequest. Those small correctness and robustness advantages put impl-2 first, narrowly.

v.rationale:
I ranked impl-2 first (8.6) and impl-1 second (7.8). Both suites pass: 31 tests for impl-2, 30 for impl-1.

The two implementations are nearly the same design: an enum cast, an observer for the unique slug and published_at, a policy enforced through ->can() route middleware, form requests, a resource that plucks tag names, and user()->posts() scoping. Both meet every requirement.

My probes covered six edge cases on each. Both handle these the same way: un-publishing and re-publishing keeps the original published_at, a guest request without JSON headers gets 401, and null fields or non-string tags get 422.

They differ in a few places:
- **Empty filters:** `?status=&tag=` returns 422 in impl-1 because its index rules aren't nullable. impl-2 ignores blank filters and has a test for it.
- **Tag creation:** impl-1 uses firstOrCreate, which can race against the unique tag-name index. impl-2 uses createOrFirst, which is safe.
- **Rule duplication:** impl-1 copies the store rules into UpdatePostRequest. impl-2 extends StorePostRequest and overrides only title and body.
- **Tag limits:** impl-2 caps tags at 20 and adds a distinct rule; impl-1 has neither.
- **Other idioms:** impl-2 binds routes by slug, loads only tag id and name, and keeps its scopes non-nullable, putting the optional-filter logic in when() in the controller.

impl-2 has a few weaknesses of its own. Its routes file splits apiResource() and a separate group, which is clumsier than impl-1's single group. Its postData() wrapper adds little.

Neither has a serious bug. impl-2 wins on robustness and on how it uses Laravel's idioms.

v.rationale: Both use nearly the same core design: Cache::flexible with versioned per-team keys, after-commit observers, and a cache lock with double-checking plus a cooldown and a last-known fallback for rates. Both suites pass (30 and 31 tests). Probes: DB::transaction invalidation, non-ASCII codes, the stale-after-an-hour flow, and plain guest GETs all behave correctly in both. impl-1 ranks first because its API is actually usable: it installs Sanctum, while impl-2 puts a session guard on a stateless API route. impl-1 also covers membership changes, uses UUID versions, and sets connectTimeout and baseUrl. I rank impl-2 first. Both implementations pass their own test suites (impl-2: 22 tests, impl-1: 19).

**Why impl-2 is better:**
- **More Laravel-idiomatic:** It checks the CSV header in the form request and rejects a bad file with a 422 before anything is stored.
- **Uses the framework's validation:** Each row goes through Laravel's Validator, with upper limits that match the database columns.
- **Correct CSV parsing:** It reads rows with fgetcsv, so quoted fields that contain newlines are handled.
- **Modern Laravel:** It uses the job attributes, a queued summary email and dispatch()->afterCommit().

**Impl-2's real problems are small:**
- A guest request without an Accept: application/json header gets a 500 instead of a 401, because no guest redirect is configured and the app has no login route.
- A price like 9.999 is silently rounded to 10.00.
- There is some ceremony: a 'create' policy check that always passes, and the header parsing appears in two places.

**Where impl-1 does better:**
- The controller is thinner, because authorization happens in route middleware (->can()).
- The job claims each import with an atomic status update, which protects against duplicate runs.
- It installs Sanctum and handles the guest 401 case correctly.

**Why impl-1 still ranks second:**
- **Breaks quoted newlines:** It reads the file one line at a time and then parses each line, so a quoted field containing a newline is split. My probe confirmed one valid row became two failed rows with the wrong row numbers.
- **Hand-written checks:** Row validation is a set of regexes instead of Laravel's Validator, and there are no upper limits. A huge stock value or a very long name would make the database save fail. With only one try allowed, the whole import would then fail on MySQL.
- **Wrong error message:** The message 'expected 4 columns' is hard-coded, so with an extra header column it reports 'expected 4 columns, got 4'.
- **Silent failures:** A file with the wrong header is accepted (202) and then fails in the background, with no reason recorded and no email to the user.

- **Duplicates (2):** they claim each subscriber with a single conditional UPDATE on crm_sync_queued_at, plus a stale-claim timeout so failed subscribers are retried later.
- **Scheduler (3):** they set withoutOverlapping(10) so a killed container's lock expires after 10 minutes instead of 24 hours.
- **Normalisation (4):** they switch to chunkById so updated rows no longer shift the pages.

My probes showed the same results for both: after a 503 outage the job lands in failed_jobs after 3 attempts, and once the CRM recovers and the claim goes stale, the subscriber syncs. They differ in two edge cases:
- **Lock held by another worker:** impl-1 releases the job and keeps it; impl-2 deletes it.
- **Subscriber deleted before the job runs:** impl-1 discards the job; impl-2 sends it to failed_jobs.

impl-1's job code is a bit more polished and more modern: Laravel 13 attributes, MaxExceptions, releaseAfter and DeleteWhenMissingModels. But its 15-minute claim timeout is shorter than its own retry window of about 16 minutes. Its tests also never prove the failed_jobs path (symptom 1): they call handle() directly and read attributes through reflection.

impl-2 is simpler. Its claim timeout leaves a safe margin over its retry window. Its end-to-end queue:work test proves the symptom-1 fix directly, and it adds Http::preventStrayRequests(). I ranked impl-2 first. Both apps are on Laravel 13.40 and their full suites pass (impl-2: 16 tests, impl-1: 18 tests).

**Probes (run in both apps, then deleted):**
- The Monday 07:30 report is due at the right UTC time in both winter and summer.
- The nightly prune fires exactly once on both DST-change nights.
- A second dispatch of the supplier sync job is deduplicated.
- A cart updated exactly 30 days ago is kept.
- Job connection with no env set: in impl-1 the "long" queue name is the same as the default one.

One probe of mine was broken: it built the overlap lock the wrong way and errored in both apps. I judged crash recovery from the code instead. Both apps cap the overlap lock (impl-2: 3 hours, impl-1: 2 hours), so a killed run cannot block the next night.

**Main difference: the long supplier job.**
- **impl-2** gives the job its own queue, `long`, on a separate connection that waits 3000 seconds before re-offering a job. The schedule chooses that connection explicitly.
- **impl-1** creates the same kind of connection but leaves it on the `default` queue. Ordinary workers read that queue too, and they re-offer a job after only 90 seconds. So a 20–40 minute run can be handed out a second time while it is still running, which is exactly the "ran more than once" problem the task rules out.
- impl-1 also picks the connection from an environment variable with no default. If the variable is missing, the job quietly falls back to the 90-second connection.

**Where impl-1 is better:**
- More thorough tests: exact 48-hour and 30-day boundaries, a mail-rendering test, and a test that a second server cannot claim the same scheduler tick.
- It updates `.env.example` to point the cache and queue at Redis, which the cross-server locks depend on.

**impl-2's weaknesses** are small: a test whose name promises a "second copy" check but only dispatches once, an `expect(true)` filler test, and an untouched `.env.example`.

The real double-run risk in impl-1 outweighs its better tests.

I ran `php artisan test` on both: impl-1 passed 23 tests and impl-2 passed 16. I read every added or changed file, ran four throwaway probe tests against each implementation, then deleted the probe files.

The two share almost the same skeleton: the same atomic markAsPaid with afterCommit dispatch, the same queue attributes, rate-limiting middleware and retryUntil.

They differ in how the job's failure handling holds up:
- **impl-1** handles failures carefully:
  - A 422 marks the order failed directly, and an array message falls back to the response body (probe confirmed).
  - Other 4xx call fail() at once, so they are not retried.
  - failed() only changes orders whose shipment is still pending, so it cannot overwrite a sent order.

  - failed() overwrites a sent shipment as failed.
  - A 422 with an array message causes a TypeError, which leads to retries that re-POST and a wrong failure reason for ops.
  - 401/403/404 are retried instead of failing permanently.
  - The customer is never emailed if queueing the mail fails after the reference is saved.

The two share almost the same skeleton: an atomic `markAsPaid` with `afterCommit` dispatch, Backoff/MaxExceptions/Timeout job attributes, `retryUntil`, the RateLimited and WithoutOverlapping middleware, and an Idempotency-Key. So the edge cases decide the ranking. impl-1 handles the failure paths better: its `failed()` can't overwrite a sent shipment, unexpected 4xx responses fail permanently instead of being retried, and the customer still gets the email after a mail failure on a later retry. My probe ran one job twice in a 2-account run: processed_accounts became 2, the run was marked Completed and the summary went out while the second account was still unprocessed.

DispatchStatementChunk increments dispatched_accounts before Queue::bulk (app/Jobs/DispatchStatementChunk.php:41-46). If the push fails part-way, the retry increments it again and pushes duplicates. total_accounts then ends up higher than the real number of accounts, so the run can stay 'running' forever, or the duplicates inflate the processed count.

ShouldBeUnique/UniqueFor on GenerateStatement does nothing because the jobs are pushed with Queue::bulk. Queue::bulk calls push() directly and skips PendingDispatch, which is where UniqueLock gets acquired (I checked this in vendor). So the duplicate protection the code seems to provide is not there.

Deterministic generator failures are retried 3 times with 30s and 120s backoff before they are counted. That is slow and wasteful for the expensive PDF step. A probe showed 3 generate calls for one bad account.

v.rationale:
I ranked impl-1 first. Both test suites pass (impl-2: 10 tests; impl-1: 11 tests). Both use the same overall design: a dispatcher job on the default queue, per-account jobs on the 'statements' queue, and an atomic conditional-UPDATE claim of the final status.

**Impl-2.** Its idempotent per-account results table keeps failed_accounts accurate even when SQS delivers a job twice. But it breaks the requirement that the run always reaches a final status in two ways:
- **Deleted account:** the job has #[DeleteWhenMissingModels] on a serialised account. If the account is deleted mid-run, the job is dropped silently and the run stays 'running' forever. A probe confirmed this.
- **The 40k fan-out:** a single dispatcher job sends about 40k individual SQS messages, with Tries(1) and no timeout. It will very likely be killed by the worker timeout, leaving the run stuck and partly dispatched.

Impl-2 also adds a results table that grows by about 40k rows every month with no pruning.

**Impl-1.** It handles the scale requirement properly: chunked, self-chaining fan-out that sends batches through Queue::bulk (SQS SendMessageBatch). It re-fetches accounts by id, so deleted or deactivated accounts still count and the run finishes (also confirmed by probe). Its weakness is counter-based tracking. Under duplicate delivery or a retry after partial success, counts go up again: a probe showed a premature 'completed' and a duplicate owner email. Its ShouldBeUnique does nothing because Queue::bulk skips the unique lock.

**Why impl-1 wins.** Its failures need a duplicate delivery or a crash at the wrong moment. Impl-2's stuck-forever outcomes come from ordinary events (an account deleted mid-run) and from the stated 40k production volume. Impl-1's tests are also more end-to-end, running a real queue worker through retries and failed(). Impl-2 is a bit simpler and uses slightly more idiomatic attributes, but correctness under the task's main focus decides it.

Impl-1's tests are stronger too: a readiness dataset including the 15-minute boundary, delay floor and cap, and an end-to-end re-queue. Impl-1's main weakness is the global WithoutOverlapping middleware. It serialises all pushes, so at peak with a slow API there will be churn and added latency, though no data is lost. Impl-2 is simpler, but its idempotency gap is a real correctness flaw, so impl-1 ranks first.

Order::markPaid (app/Models/Order.php:43) overwrites the order's amount and currency with the provider's values, and sets currency to null when the provider omits it. A probe confirmed the order's currency was wiped. This corrupts order data and was not requested.
Order::refund (app/Models/Order.php:59) uses an unconditional update to Refunded, which is inconsistent with the guarded transitions used for the other statuses.
Uppercase signatures are accepted but empty data objects get a 422 (same as impl-1). Minor.

app/Models/WebhookEvent.php:14 and app/Models/Order.php:13 make status, error and processed_at mass-assignable.

markFailed() refuses to overwrite a Processed event (and this is tested).
Stricter ingestion validation with required_if rules per event type.

v.rationale:
Both implementations are built almost the same way: an invokable controller with createOrFirst, signature middleware, a job using the Backoff/MaxExceptions/Timeout attributes with retryUntil, WithoutOverlapping and RateLimited, conditional status transitions, a ShouldQueueAfterCommit receipt, and MassPrunable with model:prune. All tests pass in both (impl-1: 42, impl-2: 37). The probes are what separate them.

impl-2 has three real correctness bugs:
- **Failed events cannot be retried.** claim() rejects the Failed status, so running `queue:retry` on the job does nothing.
- **A missing provider field is retried as if it were transient.** If the provider response has no amount, the job hits an undefined-array-key error and retries it.
- **Order data gets overwritten.** markPaid replaces the order's amount and currency with provider data, and sets currency to null when the provider omits it.

impl-1's problems are smaller:
- failed() can flip a Processed event to Failed if it runs late.
- Signature comparison is case-sensitive, so uppercase hex is rejected.
- It adds a stuck-event sweeper the task didn't ask for, which is some extra ceremony.

impl-1 also has better tests. Its rate-limiter test exercises the middleware's behaviour (12 jobs, 10 pass, 2 released), and it includes an end-to-end HTTP-to-queue test.

impl-2 has stricter ingestion validation and a guarded markFailed. Those strengths don't outweigh its bugs, so impl-1 ranks first.

bugs: The job's idempotency guard reads the model state from when the job was deserialized (app/Jobs/ProcessWebhookEvent.php:56 `$this->event->status === Processed`), not a fresh conditional claim. A duplicate job that deserialized before the first job finished will process the event again: it calls the provider again and applies the side effects again. A probe confirmed this. The order transitions limit the damage, but the event can still be processed twice.
failed() calls markFailed unconditionally (app/Models/WebhookEvent.php:62), so a late or duplicate failure overwrites an event that is already Processed and sets it to Failed. A probe confirmed this.

The payment API is called before the order lookup (Jobs/ProcessWebhookEvent.php:70-72, the order is fetched inside apply()). Events for unknown orders therefore use up a rate-limited provider request before they fail permanently.
The X-Signature check is case-sensitive, so a valid uppercase hex signature gets a 401.
An event with an empty `data` object gets a 422, even for unknown event types.
antipatterns: app/Notifications/PaymentReceipt.php:12 implements both ShouldQueue and ShouldQueueAfterCommit. This is redundant because ShouldQueueAfterCommit already extends ShouldQueue.

app/Console/Commands/RedispatchStuckWebhookEvents.php plus its five-minute schedule (routes/console.php:13) add a recovery mechanism the task did not ask for. It has its own scope, constant coupling (RETRY_WINDOW_MINUTES + 30) and README section.
database/migrations/2026_01_01_00000*.php: no down() methods.
app/Jobs/ProcessWebhookEvent.php:98 validates payload data inside the job with Validator::make, instead of validating type-specific fields at ingestion in the FormRequest.
app/Models/WebhookEvent.php:47-64 uses forceFill/save for status writes, with no guard on the current state.
strengths: Uses createOrFirst on a unique event_id and dispatches only when wasRecentlyCreated, so the controller is thin.
The job uses WithoutOverlapping, RateLimited with a named limiter (Limit::perSecond(10)), Backoff/MaxExceptions/Timeout attributes and retryUntil, and it handles 429, 5xx and 4xx separately.
Order state changes use conditional updates (transitionTo), which prevents downgrades and duplicate receipts.
The receipt notification is queued with ShouldQueueAfterCommit inside the transaction.
Uses MassPrunable with a daily scheduled model:prune.
Has the strongest tests, including one that runs the real RateLimited middleware and checks that 10 jobs pass and 2 are released, an HTTP-to-queue end-to-end test, and 429/5xx/connection/4xx paths.
The README covers worker deployment in detail (Supervisor, retry_after vs timeout, shared cache, queue:restart).
Correctly makes webhooks/* render JSON exceptions.

bugs: bootstrap/app.php does not make webhooks/* render JSON exceptions. A signed webhook that fails validation and has no Accept: application/json header gets a 302 redirect instead of 422. A probe confirmed this. Providers will see a redirect and may retry it indefinitely.

If the provider response has no `amount` key, `(int) $details['amount']` (Jobs/ProcessWebhookEvent.php:78) throws an ErrorException. This counts as a transient failure and is retried up to MaxExceptions before the event is marked failed, so a permanent data error is treated as transient.
An event with an empty `data` object is rejected with a validation error, even for unknown event types.
antipatterns: app/Jobs/ProcessWebhookEvent.php:78 `markPaid(...) && $order->user->notify(...)` uses a short-circuit expression inside a match arm for a side effect (notify returns void), which is clever but obscure.
app/Jobs/ProcessWebhookEvent.php:56 hardcodes the handled-type list in the job, and StoreWebhookEventRequest repeats it as a comma-separated string constant.
The Backoff attribute plus retryUntil of 2 hours, with the explanatory docblock, is slightly heavier than needed.
strengths: WebhookEvent::claim() is an atomic conditional update that re-reads state, so stale or duplicate jobs never re-process an event that is already Processed or Failed. A probe confirmed this.
markFailed is guarded so a late failed() cannot overwrite Processed (and this is tested).
Looks up the order before calling the provider, so it does not spend rate-limited API calls on unknown orders.
Validates type-specific fields at ingestion with required_if in the FormRequest, and the index request has typed status()/perPage() helpers using $request->enum().
Uses modern attributes throughout (Backoff, MaxExceptions, Timeout, DeleteWhenMissingModels, Tries on the notification, #[Scope], #[Fillable]), plus the Queueable from Foundation.
The receipt uses ShouldQueueAfterCommit and is sent inside a DB transaction, and refunds use createOrFirst on a unique provider_refund_id.
The prune schedule uses onOneServer, and the README explains the shared cache, retry_after vs timeout and Supervisor config.
Signature comparison is case-insensitive and constant-time, and fails closed when no secret is configured.

v.rationale:
Both implementations follow nearly the same design: createOrFirst ingestion, a signature middleware, a job with WithoutOverlapping and RateLimited, a named 10/s limiter, Backoff/MaxExceptions/retryUntil attributes, conditional order transitions, a ShouldQueueAfterCommit receipt, MassPrunable with a daily model:prune, and an admin index protected by a policy over auth.basic. Both test suites pass (impl-2: 37 tests, impl-1: 42 tests).

The deciding difference is how each one guards against processing an event twice. impl-2 claims the event with an atomic conditional UPDATE and a refresh, and markFailed will not overwrite a Processed event. In probes it skipped a stale job without calling the provider. impl-1 checks the status on the model as it was when the job was deserialized. In probes it re-ran the provider call and the side effects for an event that was already processed, and its failed() changed a Processed event to Failed. impl-1 also calls the provider before looking up the order, and it adds an extra redispatch-stuck command and schedule the task did not ask for.

impl-2's real bug is that webhooks/* does not render JSON exceptions, so a validation failure without an Accept header returns a 302. This is less severe than impl-1's idempotency gaps. impl-1 has the better tests (a real rate-limiter behaviour test and an HTTP-to-queue end-to-end test), but that does not outweigh its correctness problems in the task's focus area. impl-2 ranks first.
